kabah.claim: When the Ka'bah was rebuilt, the Prophet and al-Abbas carried stones for it (the Prophet's age of about 35 comes from the sirah).
kabah.note: Jabir's hadith confirms the stone-carrying; the age of 35 is from Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham, not from the hadith.

kabah.claim: The Quraysh clans disputed who would set the Black Stone; they agreed the first man to arrive would judge; it was the Prophet, who put the stone on a cloth, had each clan lift a corner, and set it himself.
kabah.ref: Musnad Ahmad 15504; also Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), al-Hakim's Mustadrak
kabah.note: Shu'ayb al-Arna'ut graded Ahmad's chain sahih and al-Haythami called its narrators trustworthy. In Ahmad's wording the judge is 'the first to come out of the pass'; Ibn Ishaq has 'the first to enter by the gate of Banu Shaybah'.

kabah.claim: Quraysh ran short of funds, so the rebuilt Ka'bah left out part of the Hijr (Hatim).
kabah.note: Aisha's hadith: 'your people ran short of money (al-nafaqah)'.

kabah.claim: Before prophethood Quraysh called him al-Amin (the trustworthy).
kabah.note: In the Black Stone report they say 'al-Amin has come'. Al-Arna'ut graded the chain sahih, and the title is also standard in the sirah.

hira.claim: Before revelation he used to retreat (tahannuth) for many nights in the Cave of Hira.
hira.note: Aisha's hadith on the beginning of revelation.

hira.claim: The angel said 'Read' (Iqra'); he replied 'I am not a reader' (ma ana bi-qari'); the angel pressed him three times, then recited Qur'an 96:1-5.
hira.note: The verses themselves are at https://quran.com/96/1-5.

hira.claim: He returned trembling to Khadijah saying 'Cover me'; she said 'By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you...'.
hira.note: The hadith says 'his heart trembling' (yarjufu fu'aduh) and 'zammiluni'.

hira.claim: Khadijah took him to Waraqah ibn Nawfal, who said this was the Namus that Allah sent to Moses.
hira.note: Namus is the keeper of secrets, understood as Jibril.

hira.claim: Hira is near the top of Jabal an-Nur, about 4-5 km north-east of the Masjid al-Haram; the summit is about 642 m above sea level.
hira.ref: Wikipedia, 'Jabal al-Nour' (642 m; coordinates 21.458 N, 39.861 E)
hira.note: From the coordinates, the straight-line distance to the Ka'bah is about 5 km, bearing north-east. Sources give 3 to 6 km depending on how it is measured, so 'about 4-5 km' is safest.

safa.claim: When 26:214 was revealed he climbed as-Safa and called 'Ya Sabahah!', asked whether they would believe him about cavalry behind the hill/valley; they said they had never known him to lie; Abu Lahab said 'Perish you! Is it for this you gathered us?'; Surah al-Masad (111) was revealed.
safa.note: 'Ya Sabahah' and 'we never knew you to lie' are in Bukhari 4971. Bukhari 4770 instead has him calling the clans by name and 'we found you only truthful'.

thawr.claim: Qur'an 9:40: 'the second of two, when they were in the cave... do not grieve, Allah is with us'.
Abu Bakr: 'If one of them looked down at his feet he would see us'; the Prophet: 'What do you think of two whose third is Allah?'
They hid three nights in the Cave of Thawr; Abdullah ibn Abi Bakr brought news at night; Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazed Abu Bakr's sheep nearby and brought them milk.
thawr.note: Bukhari confirms the three nights, the news and the milk. The idea that the sheep were driven over the tracks to cover them comes from Ibn Ishaq (sirah).

thawr.claim: They hired a guide from Banu al-Dil (Banu Abd ibn Adi) who followed the religion of the Quraysh pagans; the sirah names him Abdullah ibn Urayqit (Ibn Ishaq: Ibn Arqat).
thawr.note: The hadith does not name him; the name comes from Ibn Hisham.

thawr.claim: A spider's web (and in other reports two doves) at the mouth of the cave misled the pursuers.
thawr.ref: Musnad Ahmad 3251 (Ibn Abbas, spider); doves: al-Bazzar / Ibn Asakir
thawr.note: The grading is disputed. Ibn Hajar called Ahmad's chain hasan, but the Musnad editors (al-Arna'ut et al.) graded it weak and Ahmad Shakir noted a dispute over it. Al-Albani said no sahih hadith exists about the spider and doves (al-Silsilah al-Da'ifah, vol. 3). The doves report is weaker still.

thawr.claim: They left by the lower (southern) side of Makkah to Thawr, south of the city, although Madinah lies to the north.
thawr.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham); Sahih al-Bukhari 3905 ('below Makkah', coastal road)
thawr.note: Mount Thawr lies south of Makkah. Taking the opposite direction to throw off pursuers is how the sirah explains it.

hijrah.claim: They took a westerly coastal route; the journey Makkah-Madinah was roughly 400-470 km.
hijrah.ref: Gulf News on the Saudi 'Ala Khutah' Hijrah trail (about 470 km, Thawr to Quba); Arab News 2019 (about 500 km walked)
hijrah.note: Estimates vary from 380 to 500 km. The official reconstructed trail is about 470 km, so '400-450 km' is slightly low and 'about 450-470 km' is safer.

hijrah.claim: Suraqah ibn Malik pursued them and his horse's forelegs sank into the ground.
At Umm Ma'bad's tent at Qudayd, a dry, emaciated ewe gave milk when the Prophet milked it.
hijrah.ref: al-Hakim, al-Mustadrak (Kitab al-Hijrah); al-Tabarani, al-Mu'jam al-Kabir; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat; al-Bayhaqi, Dala'il
hijrah.note: Not in Bukhari or Muslim. Secondary sources report that al-Hakim graded it sahih and al-Dhahabi agreed, while others note weak or unknown narrators. Some researchers rate it hasan through its corroborating chains. I could not check these gradings at first hand.

hijrah.claim: The Hijrah became the epoch of the Islamic calendar, adopted under Umar (c. 17 AH).
hijrah.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3934 (Sahl ibn Sa'd); Umar's council: al-Tabari, Tarikh; al-Hakim (via Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib)
hijrah.note: Bukhari confirms that the dating was counted from his arrival in Madinah. Umar's role and Ali's suggestion come from al-Tabari and al-Hakim and are reported by Ibn Hajar in Fath al-Bari.

hijrah.claim: He arrived (at Quba) on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal and stayed with Banu Amr ibn Awf.
Their guide was from Banu ad-Dil and still followed the religion of the pagan Quraysh; 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah went with them.
hijrah.note: 'Amir ibn Fuhayrah and the guide set out with them and took the coastal road. This matches entries 13-14.

hijrah.claim: He arrived at Quba on a Monday in Rabi' al-Awwal.
hijrah.note: The number is confirmed: the wording 'that was on Monday, in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal' is in 3906 (Urwah's report). This duplicates entry 21.

quba.claim: He stayed with Banu Amr ibn Awf at Quba for 'ten-odd' (14) nights and founded the mosque 'founded on taqwa'; Qur'an 9:108 refers to a mosque founded on taqwa from the first day.
quba.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3906 ('ten-odd nights'), 428 ('fourteen nights'); Sahih Muslim 1398; Qur'an 9:108
quba.note: Scholars differ on which mosque 9:108 means. In Muslim 1398 the Prophet names his own mosque in Madinah, while Ibn Abbas and many exegetes held it was Quba. Ibn Hajar and Ibn Kathir say the description fits both.

quba.claim: He carried bricks/stones while building the Prophet's Mosque (Bukhari); a separate report has him carrying stones for the Quba mosque.
quba.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3906, 428 (Prophet's Mosque); al-Tabarani, al-Kabir 24/318 via al-Shamus bint al-Nu'man (Quba)
quba.note: The Bukhari reports are about the Prophet's Mosque. The Quba report is only in al-Tabarani; al-Haythami (Majma' al-Zawa'id 5898) said its narrators are trustworthy, but it is not in the Sahihayn.

quba.claim: Madinah is ringed by black basalt lava fields (harrah), part of Harrat Rahat; its last eruption, in 1256 CE, sent lava to within a few km of the city.
quba.ref: Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, Harrat Rahat (231070)
quba.note: The hadith also speak of Madinah lying 'between its two lava tracts' (labatayha), e.g. Sahih Muslim 2047.

quba.claim: He visited the Mosque of Quba every Saturday, walking or riding.
quba.note: Ibn 'Umar's hadith. 'Every Saturday' is in Bukhari 1193 and in some of Muslim's versions (1399a mentions riding and on foot only). Bukhari 1194 adds that he prayed two rak'ahs there.

quba.claim: A prayer in the Mosque of Quba is like an 'umrah.
quba.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 324; Sunan Ibn Majah 1411 (Usayd ibn Zuhayr); Sunan Ibn Majah 1412 and Sunan al-Nasa'i 699 (Sahl ibn Hunayf)
quba.note: Al-Tirmidhi: hasan gharib. Al-Albani: sahih. Zubair Ali Za'i: hasan. Al-Dhahabi called the Usayd route munkar because Abu al-Abrad is little known, but Sahl ibn Hunayf's report supports it: 'whoever purifies himself at home, then comes and prays in the Mosque of Quba, has the reward of an umrah'. The numbers are correct.

badr.claim: The people of Madinah went out to the harrah every morning to wait for him until the midday heat drove them back.
The song 'Tala'a al-badru 'alayna' sung at his arrival.
badr.ref: al-Bayhaqi, Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (via Ibn 'A'ishah); al-Albani, al-Silsilah al-Da'ifah 598
badr.note: The chain is broken (mu'dal), as Ibn Hajar, al-Iraqi and al-Albani noted. Ibn al-Qayyim (Zad al-Ma'ad) argued that if it happened at all it was on the return from Tabuk, since Thaniyyat al-Wada' is on the Syria side. The welcome itself is sahih (Bukhari 3906, 3925).

badr.claim: Yathrib was renamed: the Prophet said Allah named Madinah 'Tabah' (Taybah); 'they call it Yathrib, and it is al-Madinah'.
badr.note: 'Madinat an-Nabi' is a later conventional name, not a name stated in these hadith.

badr.claim: Al-Bara': 'I never saw the people of Madinah rejoice at anything as they rejoiced at the Messenger of God'; even the slave girls were saying 'The Messenger of God has come'.

palm-mosque.claim: His camel knelt at the site of the mosque; the land (a date-drying yard) belonged to two orphan boys, Sahl and Suhayl, and he bought it.
palm-mosque.note: In Bukhari 428 the Banu al-Najjar refuse payment for 'their walled garden'. In 3906 he declines it as a gift and buys it from the orphans. Ibn Hajar reconciles the two.

palm-mosque.claim: The mosque was of mud brick, roofed with palm fronds, with pillars of palm trunks.
He leaned on a palm trunk for the sermon; when the minbar was made the trunk cried like a child until he came down and held it.
palm-mosque.note: Jabir's and Ibn Umar's reports; it is mutawatir in meaning.

palm-mosque.claim: The minbar was made of tamarisk wood from al-Ghabah and had three steps.
palm-mosque.note: The three steps are stated in Muslim 544a ('he made these three steps'), not in Bukhari 917.

palm-mosque.claim: Ahl al-Suffah, poor 'guests of Islam' with no family or wealth, lived at the mosque; Abu Hurayrah was closely tied to them.
palm-mosque.note: Abu Hurayrah is listed among them by Abu Nu'aym, al-Sakhawi and others, and Ibn Hajar discusses this. In the hadith he is the one sent to call them.

palm-mosque.claim: Rain leaked through the palm-frond roof and after prayer there were traces of mud and water on his forehead.
palm-mosque.note: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, on the night of the 21st of Ramadan.

qiblatayn.claim: He prayed toward Jerusalem 16 or 17 months; the change came while some were praying and they turned in the prayer.
qiblatayn.note: Bukhari 40: an unnamed mosque turned while bowing in 'Asr. Bukhari 403: the people of Quba turned during Fajr the next morning.

qiblatayn.claim: Masjid al-Qiblatayn is associated with Banu Salimah, but the sources differ on where the 'turning during prayer' happened.
qiblatayn.ref: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat (from al-Waqidi); Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari on Bukhari 40; Sahih al-Bukhari 403
qiblatayn.note: The sahih hadith do not name the mosque. Ibn Hajar says it was 'said to be' Banu Salimah, and a report from Tuwaylah bint Aslam says Banu Harithah. The story of the Prophet himself praying Zuhr at Banu Salimah is in Ibn Sa'd without an isnad. Quba is a separate, sahih report (Fajr, the next day).

qiblatayn.claim: Qur'an 2:144: 'turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram'.
Bukhari 40 and 403 are two different 'turning during prayer' reports.
qiblatayn.note: Bukhari 40: the first prayer he prayed toward the Ka'bah was 'Asr. A man who had prayed with him passed a mosque (unnamed) whose people were bowing, and they turned while still in ruku'. Ibn Hajar and al-Ayni identify it as Banu Salimah (Masjid al-Qiblatayn); other reports say Banu Harithah. Bukhari 403: the people of Quba turned during Fajr the next morning. Neither has the Prophet himself turning during a prayer.

uhud.claim: The Battle of Uhud was in Shawwal 3 AH (625 CE); about seventy Muslims were killed; Hamzah was killed by Wahshi's spear.
uhud.note: The date (Shawwal 3 AH) is from Ibn Ishaq and is generally accepted.

uhud.claim: 'Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it.'
He placed about 50 archers on a hill under Abdullah ibn Jubayr and told them not to leave 'even if you see birds snatching us'; the hill is called Jabal ar-Rumat today.
uhud.note: The order is sahih. In the sirah the hill is called 'Aynayn; 'Jabal ar-Rumat' (archers' hill) is its later popular name.

uhud.claim: 'Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it.'
uhud.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4422 (Abu Humayd, returning from Tabuk), 2889 (Anas); Sahih Muslim 1393 (Anas), 1392 (Abu Humayd)
uhud.note: Both numbers are confirmed (online editions list Muslim 1393a and 1393b). In 4422 he also says 'This is Tabah', meaning Madinah.

trench.claim: The Battle of the Trench (al-Ahzab) was in 5 AH (627 CE); the Confederate army was about 10,000.
trench.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham); Ibn Sa'd; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari on Bukhari, Kitab al-Maghazi, bab Ghazwat al-Khandaq
trench.note: Musa ibn Uqbah, quoted by Bukhari, dated it Shawwal 4 AH, but Ibn Hajar says 5 AH is the relied-upon view. The figure of 10,000 is from the sirah, and modern estimates are lower.

trench.claim: Salman al-Farisi suggested digging the trench.
trench.ref: Ibn Hisham ('it is said'); al-Waqidi, al-Maghazi; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat
trench.note: This is not in the Sahihayn and has no strong connected chain. It is widely accepted narrative detail.

trench.claim: He carried earth until dust covered the skin of his belly, and they recited rajaz verses while digging.
trench.note: The verses were by Abdullah ibn Rawahah (al-Bara'); Anas reports 'We are those who pledged to Muhammad...'.

trench.claim: He broke a hard rock (kudyah) in the trench with a pickaxe; a separate report has three strikes, each followed by a promise of conquest.
trench.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4101 (Jabir, rock); Sunan al-Nasa'i 3176 (three strikes); Musnad Ahmad 18694 (al-Bara')
trench.note: The rock itself is sahih (Bukhari 4101). Nasa'i 3176 (al-Albani: hasan) names Kisra, Caesar and Ethiopia. The Sham-Persia-Yemen wording is Ahmad 18694: Ibn Hajar called its chain hasan, but al-Arna'ut graded it weak (Maymun Abu Abdillah).

trench.claim: Forty cubits of the trench were allotted to every ten men.
trench.ref: al-Tabarani, al-Mu'jam al-Kabir 6040 (Amr ibn Awf al-Muzani); Majma' al-Zawa'id 10137
trench.note: The chain includes Kathir ibn Abdullah al-Muzani, whom the majority judged weak, and it is graded weak.

well.claim: Uthman bought the well of Rumah and made it free for the Muslims; the Prophet promised Paradise (or 'better than it in Paradise') to whoever bought/dug it.
well.ref: Jami' al-Tirmidhi 3703; Sunan al-Nasa'i 3608; Sahih al-Bukhari 2778 (mu'allaq)
well.note: Tirmidhi and al-Albani graded it hasan. Bukhari cites the 'whoever digs Rumah' wording as a suspended (ta'liq) report, which al-Daraqutni gives with a connected chain.

well.claim: Bi'r Rumah is in the al-Aqiq area, north-west of the Prophet's Mosque (about 6 km).
well.ref: Wikipedia 'Bir Rumah' (24.493 N, 39.585 E); Saudi Awqaf, Uthman well endowment
well.note: The Saudi endowments site places it in the area of al-Aqiq al-Asghar.

palms.claim: 'Whoever eats seven Ajwa dates in the morning will not be harmed that day by poison or magic.'
Ajwa is tied to Madinah: 'In the Ajwa of al-Aliyah there is healing'; another wording says 'dates from between its two lava tracts'.
palms.note: Muslim 2048 (Aisha) names al-Aliyah, the upper, southern part of Madinah.

palms.claim: Pollination of the palms: 'You know better the affairs of your world.'
palms.ref: Sahih Muslim 2363 ('A'ishah and Anas); cf. 2361 (Talhah), 2362 (Rafi' ibn Khadij)
palms.note: The exact words 'antum a'lamu bi-amri dunyakum' are in 2363. The parallel reports (2361-2362) say 'if I command you something of your religion, take it; if it is my own opinion, I am only a human being'.

aqiq.claim: At Wadi al-Aqiq he said: 'Tonight one came to me from my Lord and said: Pray in this blessed valley.'
aqiq.note: The Arabic is ati, 'one who came' or 'a messenger', and commentators identify him as Jibril. 'Visitor' is a loose paraphrase.

lanes.claim: Most of old Madinah's quarters around the mosque, with their wooden roshan windows, were cleared in the twentieth- and early twenty-first-century expansions.
lanes.ref: Wikipedia 'Al-Masjid an-Nabawi' (Saudi-era expansions and demolitions); Arab News 2017 (al-Oyayna market demolished about 30 years earlier); AGSI interview with Moath Alofi (2018)
lanes.note: Clearance was gradual: the 1950s and 1970s expansions, then mainly the King Fahd expansion of 1985-1992, with more after 2012. Figures such as '95% destroyed' are advocacy estimates, and I found no single scholarly source that quantifies the loss of the rawashin.

railway.claim: The Hejaz Railway reached Madinah on 1 September 1908; Damascus-Madinah is about 1,300 km; it was funded largely by donations; it was damaged in WWI (Arab Revolt); Madinah station is now a museum; it cut the journey from about 40 days to about 5.
railway.ref: Wikipedia 'Hejaz railway'; Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911 ed.: 1,320 km)
railway.note: Two corrections. Most donations came from within the Ottoman Empire (only about 1 in 10 from Muslims outside it). The train journey is usually given as 5 days, not 3-5. The Hejaz Railway Museum in Madinah station opened in 2006.

domes.claim: The Prophet's Mosque roof has 27 sliding domes that move on rails.
domes.ref: Wikipedia 'Al-Masjid an-Nabawi' (citing Frei Otto, Finding Form, 1996; Archnet)
domes.note: They were designed by Mahmoud Bodo Rasch / SL Rasch with Buro Happold for the King Fahd expansion (1985-1992).

domes.claim: The mosque has been rebuilt and enlarged many times (Umar, Uthman, al-Walid, al-Mahdi, Qaitbay, Abdulmejid, Saudi expansions).
The 27 sliding domes in the roof of the Prophet's Mosque belong to King Fahd's (second Saudi) expansion, begun in 1984-1985; the domes were installed in 1992.
domes.ref: SL Rasch, 'Sliding Domes' project page; Saudipedia, 'The Second Saudi Expansion of the Prophet's Mosque'
domes.note: Each dome is about 18 x 18 m and 6.3 m high, weighs about 80 tonnes, and rolls on rails along the roof in about a minute. They open after sunset to let heat out and close in the day. Saudipedia gives 1993 for completion of the expansion (SL Rasch: 1984-1994). It is safe to say 'the King Fahd expansion (completed early 1990s)'.

rawdah.claim: 'Between my house and my minbar is a garden from the gardens of Paradise.'

The historic named columns of the Rawdah: al-Mukhallaqah, also al-Hannanah (the place of the weeping palm trunk, by his prayer niche); 'A'ishah (also al-Muhajirin and al-Qur'ah: 'A'ishah said people would draw lots to pray there); at-Tawbah (Abu Lubabah's repentance); as-Sarir (where his bed was placed in i'tikaf); al-Mahras or al-Haras (where 'Ali and others kept guard); al-Wufud (where he received delegations).
rawdah.ref: al-Samhudi, Wafa' al-Wafa' (ch. 4, on the mosque); Ariffin, Architectural Conservation in Islam (2005), pp. 88-89; Sunan Ibn Majah 1774 (as-Sarir / at-Tawbah)
rawdah.note: The names and meanings agree across secondary sources (Madain Project citing Ariffin; Saudipedia; IslamicLandmarks), which go back to Ibn Zabalah and Ibn al-Najjar via al-Samhudi. I could not read al-Samhudi's text online, so treat the explanations as tradition: most rest on mursal or local reports. 'Mukhallaqah' means perfumed with khaluq, said to date from 'Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz's time. Sources differ on whether the trunk stood exactly there. Ibn Majah 1774 (Ibn 'Umar, hasan per Zubair Ali Za'i) says his bed was placed behind the Pillar of Repentance during i'tikaf. Two more are often listed: at-Tahajjud, behind Fatimah's house, and the one by the Prophet's chamber (Marba'at al-Qabr / Maqam Jibril), now enclosed. The present columns are Ottoman.

rawdah.claim: Abu Lubabah tied himself to a pillar (trunk) of the mosque in repentance until God accepted it and the Prophet himself untied him.
rawdah.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), after Banu Qurayzah, via Yazid ibn Abdullah ibn Qusayt; tafsir of Qur'an 8:27 and 9:102 (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir)
rawdah.note: Ibn Ishaq: after signalling 'slaughter' to Banu Qurayzah he tied himself to a pillar ('trunk') of the mosque for six nights. His wife untied him at each prayer. At dawn the Prophet, in Umm Salamah's house, received the acceptance, and he untied him on the way to Fajr. Ibn Hisham links 8:27 to the betrayal and 9:102 ('others who have confessed their sins') to his repentance. Ibn Abbas's tafsir report puts the tying after he stayed behind from Tabuk, with 9:102. There is no sahih hadith for it, so it is sirah.

city.claim: About 250 giant convertible umbrellas (2010-2011) shade the piazzas of the Prophet's Mosque; each covers roughly 600 m2 (about 24-26 m square), about 143,000-150,000 m2 in total.
city.ref: SL Rasch project page (150,000 m2, 600 m2 per umbrella); Wikipedia citing the Saudi Embassy (250 umbrellas, 143,000 m2)
city.note: SL Rasch designed them and Liebherr built them. Sources give the size as 24-26 m, so 'about 25 m' is fine.

city.claim: The first dome over the Prophet's grave was built in 678 AH (1279 CE) under Sultan Qalawun; the present dome dates from 1818 (Mahmud II) and was first painted green in 1837 (1253 AH).
city.ref: Wikipedia 'Green Dome' (citing Ariffin, Architectural Conservation in Islam, 2005; Petersen, Dictionary of Islamic Architecture)
city.note: The original Mamluk dome was unpainted wood. It was rebuilt after the 1481 fire (Qaitbay) and again in 1818.

boycott.claim: Quraysh and Kinanah swore an oath at Khayf Bani Kinanah (al-Muhassab) against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib: no marrying them and no trading with them until they handed over the Prophet.
boycott.note: Abu Hurayrah's hadith. The Prophet recalls the place at the Farewell Hajj (1590) and before Hunayn (3882). In 1590 one narrator says 'Banu Abd al-Muttalib', the other 'Banu al-Muttalib', and al-Bukhari says 'Banu al-Muttalib' is more accurate. Muslim 1314 names the place and the oath but not the clans.

boycott.claim: The two clans withdrew with Abu Talib into his ravine (Shi'b Abi Talib), and the boycott lasted about three years.
boycott.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), the account of the pact; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat
boycott.note: Ibn Ishaq says three years, and a line of Abu Talib's poetry has 'two or three years'. Ibn Sa'd puts the start in the seventh year of prophethood. No sahih hadith gives the length.

boycott.claim: Hakim ibn Hizam smuggled food (wheat) to his aunt Khadijah in the ravine.
boycott.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), the account of the pact
boycott.note: Abu Jahl caught him with a slave carrying wheat for Khadijah. Abu al-Bakhtari stepped in and struck Abu Jahl with a camel's jawbone. There is no isnad.

boycott.claim: The boycott document hung in the Ka'bah was eaten by termites (al-aradah) except the words 'Bismika Allahumma' (In Your name, O God).
boycott.ref: Ibn Hisham (on Ibn Ishaq), the account of the pact; al-Bayhaqi, Dala'il al-Nubuwwah (via Musa ibn Uqbah and Urwah, mursal)
boycott.note: There is no connected chain: it comes from Ibn Ishaq/Ibn Hisham and mursal maghazi reports, and is not in the sahih collections. The wording varies. Ibn Hisham has 'all except Bismika Allahumma', while the Prophet's message to Abu Talib in the same account says the termites left every name of God and ate the injustice, the cutting of ties and the slander. Safer wording: 'the sirah reports...'. The scribe is named as Mansur ibn Ikrimah (some say al-Nadr ibn al-Harith).

boycott.claim: The boycott was ended by Hisham ibn Amr, Zuhayr ibn Abi Umayyah, al-Mut'im ibn Adi, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham and Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad.
boycott.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), the account of the pact
boycott.note: The five names are correct as given by Ibn Ishaq. Hisham ibn Amr started it and Abu Jahl opposed them. In Ibn Ishaq's account al-Mut'im tore up the document.

boycott.claim: Abu Talib and Khadijah died soon after the boycott, about three years before the Hijrah. The name 'Year of Sorrow' ('Am al-Huzn) is later usage.
boycott.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3896 (Khadijah died three years before he left for Madinah); Ibn Ishaq (both died in one year); the name: IslamQA 221486 (al-Albani and Dr. al-Awshan found no isnad)
boycott.note: The deaths are well attested. Bukhari 3896 is Urwah's report, technically mursal, though Ibn Hajar thought it was likely taken from Aisha. The name 'Am al-Huzn' has no isnad to the Prophet, nor to the Companions or early imams. It first appears in later works (lexicographers via Tha'lab from Ibn al-A'rabi, then al-Qastallani and al-Sakhawi). Do not write 'the Prophet called it the Year of Sorrow'. Say 'later called the Year of Sorrow'.

isra.claim: Qur'an 17:1: 'Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa...'.
The prophets met in each heaven: Adam (1st), Yahya and 'Isa (2nd), Yusuf (3rd), Idris (4th), Harun (5th), Musa (6th), Ibrahim (7th).
isra.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3887 (Anas from Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah); Sahih Muslim 162 (Anas)
isra.note: The list and order are exactly as in Bukhari 3887. Note that Abu Dharr's version (Bukhari 349) places Ibrahim in the sixth heaven and does not give the heavens of Idris, Musa and 'Isa, so use 3887 for the sequence.

isra.claim: Sidrat al-Muntaha (the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary).
isra.note: 53:14 is 'by the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary'. Bukhari 3887 also describes it on the Mi'raj.

isra.claim: Fifty prayers were reduced to five at Musa's urging, with the reward of fifty.
isra.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3887 (reduction), 349 ('they are five and they are fifty')
isra.note: In 3887 the reduction is in steps (50, 40, 30, 20, 10, 5), ending with 'I have carried out My obligation and lightened it for My servants'. The words 'five, and they are fifty' and 'My word does not change' are in Abu Dharr's version (349), where the reduction is by halves.

isra.claim: The date is disputed; a common view puts the Isra' about a year before the Hijrah.
isra.ref: Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat; Ibn Hajar, Fath al-Bari (Kitab Manaqib al-Ansar, bab al-Mi'raj)
isra.note: Ibn Hajar lists more than ten opinions, ranging from about five years after the first revelation to six months before the Hijrah. 'One year before' is attributed to Ibn Sa'd and others, and Ibn Hazm claimed consensus, which others reject. The popular date of 27 Rajab has no firm basis. Keep the wording 'scholars differ'.

aqabah.claim: First Pledge of al-Aqabah: twelve men pledged not to associate anything with God, steal, commit adultery, kill their children, bring slander, or disobey him in what is right (the 'pledge of women', before fighting was prescribed).
aqabah.ref: Musnad Ahmad 22754 and Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), both from 'Ubadah ibn as-Samit; cf. Sahih al-Bukhari 18
aqabah.note: Bukhari 18 gives the terms and identifies 'Ubadah as a naqib of the night of al-Aqabah, but it does not say 'first pledge' or 'twelve'. Ibn Hajar argues that the pledge in Bukhari 18 itself was a later one, after the conquest. The 'twelve men' and the link of these terms to the First Aqabah come from Ibn Ishaq's report (Yazid ibn Abi Habib, Marthad al-Yazani, al-Sunabihi, 'Ubadah), recorded by Ahmad 22754, which al-Arna'ut graded sahih. A parallel in al-Hakim says eleven.

aqabah.claim: Mus'ab ibn Umayr was sent to Madinah after the First Pledge to teach the Qur'an; he and Ibn Umm Maktum were the first of the emigrants to come to the Ansar.
aqabah.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3925, 3924 (al-Bara'); Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham) for his being sent after the First Pledge
aqabah.note: Wording fix: al-Bara' says 'the first to come to us were Mus'ab ibn Umayr and Ibn Umm Maktum, and they taught the people the Qur'an', so Mus'ab was not alone. Ibn Ishaq names Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Asad as the first Makkan emigrant to reach Madinah, a year before the pledge. Better: 'among the first to arrive, sent to teach'.

aqabah.claim: Second Pledge: seventy-odd men and two women (Nusaybah bint Ka'b and Asma' bint Amr) met him at night at al-Aqabah and pledged to protect him as they protected their own women and children.
aqabah.ref: Musnad Ahmad 15798 (Ka'b ibn Malik, via Ibn Ishaq); Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham): seventy-three men and two women
aqabah.note: Al-Arna'ut: 'a strong hadith, and this chain is hasan'. Ahmad's text says 'we were seventy men' and names the two women. The figure 'seventy-three men and two women' is Ibn Ishaq's (Ibn Hisham). The terms are 'protect me from what you protect your women and children from'. 'About seventy-three men and two women' is fine if you attribute it to the sirah.

aqabah.claim: Masjid al-Bay'ah at the site of the pledge was built by the Abbasid caliph Abu Ja'far al-Mansur in 144 AH (761-762 CE).
aqabah.ref: Saudipedia 'Al-Bay'ah Mosque'; Wikipedia 'Bay'ah Mosque' (two inscriptions, on the qiblah and southern walls)
aqabah.note: The inscriptions also record a restoration by the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir (reigned 623-640 AH; one source gives 625 AH). It lies in a pass of Thabir near the Jamrat al-Aqabah in Mina.

conquest.claim: He set out for Makkah in Ramadan with about ten thousand men.
There were 360 idols around the Ka'bah; he struck them with a stick in his hand, reciting 'Truth has come and falsehood has vanished' (Qur'an 17:81).
conquest.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4287, 4720, 2478 (Ibn Mas'ud); Sahih Muslim 1781; Qur'an 17:81, 34:49
conquest.note: He also recited 34:49 ('Truth has come, and falsehood neither begins nor returns'). The verses are at https://quran.com/17/81.

conquest.claim: 'Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe; whoever lays down his arms is safe; whoever locks his door is safe.'
conquest.note: Online editions list it as 1780a; the printed (Abd al-Baqi) number is 1780. The Abu Sufyan line is also in Sunan Abi Dawud 3021 (Ibn Abbas; al-Albani: hasan).

conquest.claim: Bilal gave the call to prayer from the roof of the Ka'bah on the day of the conquest.
conquest.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham), from 'some of the family of Jubayr ibn Mut'im'; Urwah (mursal), cited in al-Dhahabi, Siyar 2/181; Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat
conquest.note: This is well known in the sirah but rests on mursal or incomplete chains. It is not in the sahih collections. The story that Abu Bakr and Umar lifted Bilal up has no known isnad. Present it as 'the sirah reports'.

conquest.ref: Ibn Ishaq (Ibn Hisham 2/412: 'some of the people of knowledge told me'); al-Tabari, Tarikh; al-Albani, al-Silsilah al-Da'ifah 1163
conquest.note: This exact sentence has weak chains: Ibn Ishaq's source is unnamed, and the other route is mursal or includes weak narrators. The general pardon of the Makkans is well established, and the term 'al-tulaqa'' for those freed at the conquest is in sahih hadith (e.g. Sahih al-Bukhari 4333, Anas on the day of Hunayn). If the scene quotes it, mark it as 'reported in the sirah'.

arafat.claim: The Farewell Sermon at 'Arafah: 'Your blood and your property are sacred...'; 'Fear God concerning women'; 'I have left among you... the Book of God'; 'O God, bear witness'.
arafat.note: Wording fix: in Muslim 1218 he asks 'You will be asked about me; what will you say?' They answer 'We bear witness that you have conveyed...', and he says 'O God, bear witness' three times, pointing his finger to the sky and then to the people. The question 'Have I conveyed?' (a la hal ballaghtu) is from the sermon at Mina on the Day of Sacrifice (Sahih al-Bukhari 1739, 1741), not from Jabir's 'Arafah text. Jabir places the sermon in the bottom of the valley (Batn al-Wadi, i.e. 'Uranah, near today's Masjid Namirah), not on the hill. Afterwards he stood at the rocks at the foot of the hill.

arafat.claim: 'Let the one present convey to the one absent.'
arafat.note: Place fix: this was said on the Day of Sacrifice (10 Dhu al-Hijjah) at Mina, not at 'Arafah. Bukhari 67 asks 'Is it not the Day of Nahr?', and Ibn Hajar and al-Ayni place it at Mina. If the 'Arafat scene uses it, say it was part of the Farewell Hajj sermons at Mina.

arafat.claim: Qur'an 5:3 ('This day I have perfected your religion for you') was revealed on the Day of 'Arafah, a Friday, while the Prophet was standing at 'Arafat.
The name 'Jabal ar-Rahmah' (Mount of Mercy) is later usage; the hill was anciently called Ilal.
arafat.ref: IslamQA 34154 (Ibn Uthaymin: the name has no basis in the Sunnah); 'Atiq al-Biladi via IslamOnline (old name Ilal); Saudipedia 'Jabal al-Rahmah'
arafat.note: Classical sources call it Ilal (also al-Qurayn); the hadith call it simply 'the mountain' or the rocks (al-sakharat) at 'Arafah. I did not find when 'Jabal ar-Rahmah' first came into use, so 'later name' is the safe wording.
